title: How To Manage Voice Levels In Your Classroom https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/02/23/how-to-manage-voice-levels-in-your-classroom/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents a simple numbered system (0 through 3) for defining and teaching acceptable voice levels for different classroom activities, from silent reading to outdoor games. He explains each level's appropriate use, and prefers this system over proximity-based rules (like '12-inch voices'), which he finds confusing and harder to define. He addresses the natural tendency for volume to creep up during small-group work, advising teachers not to overreact but to pause, reset with deep breaths, and only invoke the classroom management plan for clear violations like whispering turning into normal talk. He stresses that each level must be thoroughly taught, modeled, and rehearsed before being expected in practice.
points: Presents a four-level voice system: 0 (no talking), 1 (whispering), 2 (conversation), 3 (have fun/outdoor activity).
Prefers numbered voice levels over proximity-based systems (e.g., '12-inch voices'), which are harder to define and more confusing for students.
Volume naturally creeps up during level-2 group work; the fix is a brief pause and reset, not anger or lecturing.
Straying from a designated level (e.g., whispering becoming normal talk) should be addressed via the classroom management plan, not tolerated as a natural phenomenon.
Each level must be thoroughly taught, modeled, and rehearsed through scenarios before students are expected to use it independently.
quotes: Like so much of classroom management, the key to managing voice levels is to define for your students what you expect of them—and then hold them to it.
The idea is to standardize a few simple volume levels for your classroom, teach them to your students, and then clarify for each activity which level is appropriate.

Some teachers prefer to define voice levels by proximity. In other words, they'll ask students to speak in 12-inch or 36-inch voices, for example. But this can be confusing to students and difficult to define.
Getting angry and lecturing in response is a mistake that discourages wonderful and beneficial collaboration and learning.

There is no natural phenomenon at work when students stop whispering and begin using normal speaking voices. In this case, and in any case of straying from a designated level, just follow your classroom management plan.
Therefore, it’s important—and only fair—to thoroughly teach, model, and role-play each level before putting the strategy into practice.
